title: The Basel Framework - Bank for International Settlements
summary: The Basel Framework is the comprehensive set of prudential banking standards published by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (BCBS), representing the full corpus of global banking regulation standards. The document encompasses capital requirements, risk-based capital calculations, market risk frameworks, counterparty credit risk treatment, and leverage ratio specifications. This is a foundational reference document rather than a specific policy event or market catalyst.
key_points: Contains the complete Basel Framework standards including capital definition (CAP), risk-based capital requirements (RBC), credit risk (CRE), market risk (MAR), operational risk (OPE), and leverage ratio (LEV) sections
Includes market risk framework (MAR) covering standardised approach, internal models approach, backtesting requirements, and credit valuation adjustment framework
Contains counterparty credit risk definitions and capital treatment for central counterparties (CRE54, CRE55)
Specifies minimum haircut floors for securities financing transactions (CRE56)
Defines boundary between banking book and trading book (RBC25)
Covers cryptoasset exposures under the prudential framework (SCO60)
why_it_matters: This document is the authoritative reference for global banking prudential standards. While not a specific market catalyst, it contains elements relevant to market structure including market risk capital requirements, securities financing transaction haircut floors, and trading book/banking book boundaries—all of which affect how banks manage and report market-related exposures.
market_structure_context: The document contains market structure-relevant elements including: (1) Market risk capital requirements framework defining trading desk boundaries, standardised approach, and internal models methodology; (2) Counterparty credit risk definitions and capital treatment for central counterparties; (3) Minimum haircut floors for securities financing transactions; (4) Trading book versus banking book boundary definitions. These elements influence how banks structure their market-facing activities and affect securities financing market dynamics.
